THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: The 2Gbps UDP flow keeps the sender-side FIFO queue full, so TCP packets are dropped before TCP can deliver payload.
  [Y2] guess: The 100-packet FIFO queue length is the proximate cause: a much shorter queue would reduce persistent fullness and allow some TCP packets through.
  [Y3] guess: TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth.
  [Y4] guess: FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps.
  [Y5] guess: Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.
  [Y6] guess: The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.
  [Y7] guess: The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.
  [Y8] guess: TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions.
  [H1] hypothesis (refuted): Reducing l1.queue.length from 100 to 4 while keeping TcpCubic increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
  [H2] hypothesis (refuted): Changing tcp.type from TcpCubic to TcpBbr while keeping l1.queue.length=100 increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: The 2Gbps UDP flow keeps the sender-side FIFO queue full, so TCP packets are dropped before TCP can deliver payload.
  [Y2] guess: The 100-packet FIFO queue length is the proximate cause: a much shorter queue would reduce persistent fullness and allow some TCP packets through.
  [Y3] guess: TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth.
  [Y4] guess: FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps.
  [Y5] guess: Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.
  [Y6] guess: The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.
  [Y7] guess: The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.
  [Y8] guess: TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions.
  [Y9] guess: FIFO TCP is RTO-stalled: cwnd can open but only one segment stays unacked, so exponential RTO dominates and payload delivery is zero.
  [Y10] guess: Scheduler gives TCP an equal service share; goodput is set by that share and packet overhead, not by TCP variant or larger queue.
  [Y11] guess: Reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic, low enough that the receiver-side queue never fills.
  [Y12] guess: Under scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing could let TCP exceed the equal-share payload rate, so tcp.type matters.

Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: The 2Gbps UDP flow keeps the sender-side FIFO queue full, so TCP packets are dropped before TCP can deliver payload.
  [Y2] guess: The 100-packet FIFO queue length is the proximate cause: a much shorter queue would reduce persistent fullness and allow some TCP packets through.
  [Y3] guess: TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth.
  [Y4] guess: FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps.
  [Y5] guess: Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.
  [Y6] guess: The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.
  [Y7] guess: The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.
  [Y8] guess: TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions.
  [Y9] guess: FIFO TCP is RTO-stalled: cwnd can open but only one segment stays unacked, so exponential RTO dominates and payload delivery is zero.
  [Y10] guess: Scheduler gives TCP an equal service share; goodput is set by that share and packet overhead, not by TCP variant or larger queue.
  [Y11] guess: Reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic, low enough that the receiver-side queue never fills.
  [Y12] guess: Under scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing could let TCP exceed the equal-share payload rate, so tcp.type matters.
  [Y13] guess: A larger scheduler queue would reduce TCP drops further and could raise tcp_goodput_bps above the length-100 value.
  [Y14] guess: Under scheduler, tcp_goodput_bps is set by how fully the congestion control keeps its per-flow scheduler service share filled; loss-based Cubic-like variants fill it, while Bbr underfills it.
  [Y15] guess: One of TcpBic, TcpLinuxReno, or TcpNewReno fills the scheduler share better than TcpCubic and gives more than 1% higher tcp_goodput_bps.
  [Y16] guess: TcpVegas's delay-based probing may avoid loss-induced backoff and fill the scheduler's per-flow share more steadily, giving more than 1% higher tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic.
  [H1] hypothesis (refuted): Reducing l1.queue.length from 100 to 4 while keeping TcpCubic increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
  [H2] hypothesis (refuted): Changing tcp.type from TcpCubic to TcpBbr while keeping l1.queue.length=100 increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
  [H3] hypothesis (inconclusive): Replacing the sender-side FIFO queue on l1 with a scheduler queue while keeping default settings increases tcp_goodput_bps above the default value.
  [H4] hypothesis (dropped): At the same l1.queue.length (4 and 100) and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher tcp_goodput_bps than a FIFO queue.
  [H5] hypothesis (dropped): At l1.queue.length=100 and TcpCubic, a sender-side scheduler queue gives higher mean tcp_bps than a FIFO queue.

The result it starts from, as the researcher states it: TcpBic has tcp_retrans=1901 and TcpNewReno has tcp_retrans=43 while both deliver about 482 Mbps.
The guess of why: The retransmission spread reflects different average TCP inflight/service consumption by the variants, not merely different loss timing within the same service share.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: The 2Gbps UDP flow keeps the sender-side FIFO queue full, so TCP packets are dropped before TCP can deliver payload.
  [Y2] guess: The 100-packet FIFO queue length is the proximate cause: a much shorter queue would reduce persistent fullness and allow some TCP packets through.
  [Y3] guess: TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth.
  [Y4] guess: FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps.
  [Y5] guess: Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.
  [Y6] guess: The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.
  [Y7] guess: The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.
  [Y8] guess: TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions.
  [Y9] guess: FIFO TCP is RTO-stalled: cwnd can open but only one segment stays unacked, so exponential RTO dominates and payload delivery is zero.
  [Y10] guess: Scheduler gives TCP an equal service share; goodput is set by that share and packet overhead, not by TCP variant or larger queue.
  [Y11] guess: Reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic, low enough that the receiver-side queue never fills.
  [Y12] guess: Under scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing could let TCP exceed the equal-share payload rate, so tcp.type matters.
  [Y13] guess: A larger scheduler queue would reduce TCP drops further and could raise tcp_goodput_bps above the length-100 value.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.

  [Y3] (refuted by V2) TcpCubic's loss-based response to UDP-induced drops makes TCP back off, while TcpBbr could maintain inflight and obtain bandwidth. | competes with Y2
  [Y4] (revised as Y5) FIFO scheduling lets UDP monopolize the link; a scheduler queue that gives each flow an equal link share would raise tcp_goodput_bps. | competes with Y2
  [Y5] (revised as Y10) Per-flow scheduling gives TCP a service share, so TCP goodput is set by that share and packet overhead rather than by FIFO queue length or TCP variant.
  [Y6] (refuted by V4) The scheduler result is caused by its 100-packet per-flow buffering; with l1.queue.length=4 the scheduler would starve TCP like FIFO.
  [Y7] (revised as Y11) The reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic from the scheduler-given TCP flow; ACK volume is low enough that the receiver-side queue drops none.
  [Y8] (revised as Y9) TCP is stalled in persistent RTO: FIFO tail drops its initial/probe segments, cwnd stays minimal, and exponential RTO limits it to a few retransmissions. | competes with Y1
  [Y9] FIFO TCP is RTO-stalled: cwnd can open but only one segment stays unacked, so exponential RTO dominates and payload delivery is zero.
  [Y10] (refuted by V5) Scheduler gives TCP an equal service share; goodput is set by that share and packet overhead, not by TCP variant or larger queue.
  [Y11] Reverse utilization is TCP ACK traffic, low enough that the receiver-side queue never fills.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.

THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.
THE SETTINGS THE RESEARCHER MAY CHANGE: l1.queue.length (4 to 1000, default 100); tcp.type (TcpBbr, TcpBic, TcpCubic, TcpLinuxReno, TcpNewReno, TcpVegas, default TcpCubic)
THE NETWORK MAY CHANGE TOO: in this brief a simulation may change the structure of the network (add or remove hosts, links, flows and queues), as a legitimate way to test a guess; at most 2 hosts, 1 link, 2 flows; never removed: host:sender, flow:udp, link:l1, host:receiver, flow:tcp. A planned simulation's change is shown with it (network changed: ...).
TOLERANCE: 1 %: in a decision rule == holds for two values closer than that; <, <=, > and >= compare the numbers as measured, and a check that two measured results decide by less is marked.

THE GUESS of why it came out so: Under the scheduler, TCP delivered goodput is set by the average service share it obtains; loss-based variants fill the queue and incur TCP drops, and retransmissions recover those drops while consuming the same service share, so their different retransmission counts can leave delivered goodput nearly unchanged, while Vegas avoids drops and keeps queue occupancy low, so it obtains a smaller service share and delivers lower TCP goodput despite zero retransmissions.
THE HYPOTHESIS H12: With a sender-side scheduler at l1.queue.length=100, TcpBic and TcpNewReno have mean tcp_inflight within 10% of each other despite tcp_retrans=1901 and 43.
DECISION RULE: abs(tcp_inflight_mean@bic100 - tcp_inflight_mean@newreno100) <= 0.10 * tcp_inflight_mean@newreno100
